summary: Manager one-to-one held immediately before the daily team meeting. Richard reports on two high-performer calls from earlier that day: one where the prospect asked for a contract and left mid-call with an agreement sent and a follow-up promised the same evening, and one where the prospect said 'give me till next week' and 'don't pressure me', which Richard chose not to work. They review the second call from the price drop. Chris corrects two things — Richard reading from his notes on camera, and the way he answered a direct question about splitting the payment — and gives him the scripted money-objection opening verbatim. The second half of the session is not sales coaching at all: Chris runs Richard through a worst-case-scenario ladder (missing projections, being taken off priority, being fired, running out of savings, moving back into his parents' house in the Netherlands), surfaces that the charge underneath it is shame about proving something to his father, and then leads a guided breathing and somatic acceptance exercise for roughly three minutes. It closes with Chris reframing the sales frame as 'play to serve' rather than 'play not to lose'.
notable: INSTALMENTS CARRY INTEREST, CONFIRMED ON A LIVE CALL: the prospect asked "if I don't want to spend the 6K at once, is it possible to split it, if it's always six months, to do 6K in six months?" and Richard answered "It would be a little bit more because there's interest with that." This corroborates the $7,200 six-instalment figure quoted to Manish the same day.

COACHED RESPONSE TO A PAYMENT-PLAN QUESTION: Chris said Richard's answer was wrong — "That is not the way you would respond to that" — and gave the replacement verbatim: "I usually immediately say, yeah, I hear you. Most guys usually just throw it on a credit card, take care of it that way. But why do you ask? Do you, like, need a payment plan?" He then recited the full isolation sequence and told Richard "You can, you literally should have that memorized."

Richard deliberately skipped the Phase 5 consequence frame on a high performer, applying the previous day's coaching: "I skipped, like, the bad outcome aspect, because I saw with him, he was already dedicated to do it."

A prospect explicitly refused to be worked: "he said, like, yeah, well, give me till next week. And I was like, dude, do you need till next week? Well, don't pressure me." Richard chose not to run objection handling because "then he is just going to tell me to screw off."
Richard texted a waiting prospect that he was "currently onboarding a new client" while he was in fact still on an unclosed sales call with the previous prospect.

Richard did not know whether the company could provide a contract before asking for one on a live call: "I didn't even know if I could get a contract, so I was curious, I didn't even know it myself, but he was quite surprised by that."

CONSEQUENCES OF MISSING PROJECTIONS, IN THE REP'S OWN WORDS: "the worst case would be that I would get taken off priority, which I don't want to", followed by being fired. Chris did not correct or soften the framing, he used it as the start of an acceptance exercise.

Chris's diagnosis of why calls are lost is nervous-system state rather than tactics: "the person that has the more calm, relaxed nervous system is the one who's generating more certainty, and they are the one that leads the call", and Richard agreed the prospect was the calmer party.

Richard identified a concrete mechanical cause he can fix: he took a call back to back with no gap and "started the call with way too fast-paced energy", and says he should have left the prospect in the waiting room for a few minutes to reset.

The session's closing frame is a genuinely good one for the audit to note against the harder tactics elsewhere in the corpus: "instead of playing not to lose, play to serve... if the prospect can feel like it's a win for them, they want you to get the commission. So focus on them, and the win will come to you."
